lessons.title: Explore Relationships Between Two Variables
lessons.objective: I can recognize when two quantities change together, and identify which one is the independent variable and which is the dependent variable.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain which quantity depends on the other using the words independent variable, dependent variable, and depends on.

concept.heading: Which quantity is doing the changing — and which is responding?
concept.intro: When two quantities are related, one of them depends on the other. Naming which is which is the whole job of this lesson.
concept.keyIdea: Independent & Dependent Variables. 1. Independent Variable (x): The input / cause that is chosen or changes freely. 2. Dependent Variable (y): The output / effect that depends on the independent variable. 3. Sentence check: 'The (dependent) depends on the (independent)'

worked.title: Watch me sort Akela's experiment
lines: The two quantities are hours of sunlight per day and average plant height after 3 weeks.
Akela CHOSE where to put each tray, so she chose the sunlight. Sunlight is subject to choice — that makes it the independent variable.
She did not choose how tall the plants got. Height responded. That makes height the dependent variable.
Say it as a sentence: plant height depends on sunlight.
linesEs: Las dos cantidades son las horas de luz solar al día y la altura promedio de la planta después de 3 semanas.
Akela eligió dónde poner cada charola, así que eligió la luz solar. La luz solar está sujeta a elección — eso la hace la variable independiente.
Ella no eligió qué tan altas crecieron las plantas. La altura respondió. Eso hace que la altura sea la variable dependiente.
Dilo como una oración: la altura de la planta depende de la luz solar.
worked.titleEs: Mírame clasificar el experimento de Akela

together.title: Let's try Claire's fitness tracker together
lines: Claire burned 123 Calories on a 30-minute jog and 246 Calories on a 60-minute jog.
Which did Claire choose — the minutes, or the Calories?
She chose how long to jog. So time is independent, and Calories burned is dependent.
linesEs: Claire quemó 123 calorías en una carrera de 30 minutos y 246 calorías en una de 60 minutos.
¿Qué eligió Claire — los minutos o las calorías?
Ella eligió cuánto tiempo correr. Así que el tiempo es independiente, y las calorías quemadas son dependientes.
together.titleEs: Probemos juntos con el rastreador de Claire

vocabulary.definition: The input quantity in a model, chosen or observed.
vocabulary.example: Miguel picks the number of MONTHS — nothing else decides it for him.

vocabulary.definition: The quantity that changes in response to the independent variable.
vocabulary.example: Total cost = $24.95 × months — the cost RESPONDS to the months.

vocabulary.definition: One quantity depends on another when changing the first causes the second to change.
vocabulary.example: “Total cost depends on the number of months.” Responder first, chooser last.

vocabulary.definition: Something that can be counted or measured.
vocabulary.example: 24.95 dollars per month, 12 months — each is a number with a meaning.

vocabulary.definition: How two quantities change together.
vocabulary.example: 1 month → $24.95, 2 months → $49.90: the two quantities move together.

vocabulary.definition: A list of matched input and output pairs.
vocabulary.example: x: 2, 4 paired with y: 14, 28

vocabulary.definition: The independent value you put in; it fills the first column of a table.
vocabulary.example: Minutes jogged

vocabulary.definition: The dependent value that comes out; it fills the second column of a table.
vocabulary.example: Calories burned

lessons.title: Analyze Graphs of Relationships Between Two Variables
lessons.objective: I can use a table and a graph to determine and analyze the relationship between two variable quantities.
lessons.languageObjective: I can describe what a point on a graph represents using the words ordered pair, axis, and coordinates.

concept.heading: Two pictures of the same relationship
concept.intro: A table shows a relationship with numbers. A graph shows the same relationship with points. Reading either one tells you how the dependent variable responds to the independent variable.
concept.keyIdea: Representing Two-Variable Relationships with Tables & Graphs. Formula: Table (x, y) → Graph Point (x, y). 1. Construct table: Put independent variable in column 1 (x) and dependent in column 2 (y). 2. Identify the rate of change or rule connecting x to y. 3. Plot the ordered pairs on the coordinate plane with x on horizontal axis and y on vertical

worked.title: Watch me build the ticket graph
lines: Each ticket costs $45, so the total cost is 45 times the number of tickets: 1 ticket is $45, 2 tickets are $90, 3 tickets are $135.
The number of tickets is the independent variable, so it goes first in each ordered pair: (1, 45), (2, 90), (3, 135).
I label one axis 'Number of tickets' and the other 'Total cost ($)', then plot each pair as a point.
The points rise to the right: as the number of tickets increases, the total cost increases.
linesEs: Cada boleto cuesta $45, así que el costo total es 45 por el número de boletos: 1 boleto son $45, 2 boletos son $90, 3 boletos son $135.
El número de boletos es la variable independiente, así que va primero en cada par ordenado: (1, 45), (2, 90), (3, 135).
Rotulo un eje como «Número de boletos» y el otro como «Costo total ($)», y luego marco cada par como un punto.
Los puntos suben hacia la derecha: conforme aumenta el número de boletos, aumenta el costo total.
worked.titleEs: Mírame armar la gráfica de los boletos

together.title: Let's graph the Sandia Peak tram together
lines: The tram travels 1,200 feet every minute. Which quantity is independent — time or distance?
Time is independent, so our pairs look like (minutes, feet): (1, 1200), (2, 2400), (5, 6000).
The ascent takes 15 minutes, so the last point is (15, 18000) — because 15 times 1,200 is 18,000 feet.
Each point means: after THIS many minutes, the tram has traveled THIS many feet.
linesEs: El teleférico recorre 1,200 pies cada minuto. ¿Qué cantidad es independiente — el tiempo o la distancia?
El tiempo es independiente, así que nuestros pares se ven como (minutos, pies): (1, 1200), (2, 2400), (5, 6000).
El ascenso toma 15 minutos, así que el último punto es (15, 18000) — porque 15 por 1,200 son 18,000 pies.
Cada punto significa: después de estos minutos, el teleférico ha recorrido estos pies.
together.titleEs: Grafiquemos juntos el teleférico de Sandia Peak

vocabulary.definition: A picture on a coordinate plane that shows how two quantities are related.
vocabulary.example: Points (1, 45), (2, 90), (3, 135) climbing left to right — cost by tickets.

vocabulary.definition: A list of matched pairs of values that shows a relationship using numbers.
vocabulary.example: months 1, 2, 4 beside cost 24.95, 49.90, 99.80 — one row per pair.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers written as (x, y) that name one point on a graph. The independent variable comes first.
vocabulary.example: (3, 135): 3 tickets cost $135 — the independent quantity comes first.

vocabulary.definition: One of the two number lines that frame a graph. Each axis is labeled with a quantity from the problem.
vocabulary.example: Horizontal axis: months. Vertical axis: total cost.

vocabulary.definition: The numbers in an ordered pair that tell how far to move along each axis to reach a point.
vocabulary.example: In (4, 105), 4 says how far across and 105 how far up.

vocabulary.definition: How much y changes each time x goes up by one.
vocabulary.example: Up $4 for each hour.

vocabulary.definition: The point (0, 0) where the two axes meet.

support.prompt: Akela chooses how many hours of sunlight each tray gets. Which is the INDEPENDENT variable?
support.explanation: Akela chooses the sunlight, so sunlight is subject to choice — that makes it independent.
feedback: You have the two variables backward. Ask which one someone gets to CHOOSE — that one is independent.
The number of trays is not one of the two quantities being related here.
The number of seeds is not one of the two quantities being related here.
hints: Which quantity did Akela get to decide?
Sunlight was set by where she put the tray.
The one subject to choice is independent.

support.prompt: In Akela's experiment, which is the DEPENDENT variable?
support.explanation: Height responds to how much sunlight the tray received, so height is the dependent variable.
feedback: You have the two variables backward. Ask which one someone gets to CHOOSE — that one is independent.
The kind of seed was the same for all three trays.
The tray size was the same for all three trays.
hints: Which quantity RESPONDED to the other?
Akela did not choose how tall the plants grew.
The responding quantity is dependent.

support.prompt: Claire burned 123 Calories on a 30-minute jog. Which quantity is subject to choice?
support.explanation: Claire decides how long to jog. The Calories follow from that decision.
feedback: You have the two variables backward. Ask which one someone gets to CHOOSE — that one is independent.
Heart rate is not one of the two quantities in this problem.
The weather is not one of the two quantities in this problem.
hints: What does Claire decide before she starts?
She sets the time on the tracker.
Calories are the result, not the choice.

support.prompt: Which sentence is written in the correct order?
choices: Minutes jogged depends on Calories burned.
Calories burned depends on Calories burned.
Neither quantity depends on the other.
Calories burned depends on minutes jogged.
support.explanation: The dependent quantity comes first in the sentence '___ depends on ___ .' Calories respond to time, so Calories depend on minutes.
feedback: You have the two variables backward. Ask which one someone gets to CHOOSE — that one is independent.
A quantity cannot depend on itself.
These two quantities are clearly related — more time means more Calories.
hints: Say both versions out loud. Which one is true?
Claire chooses the minutes.
The responder goes first: 'responder depends on chooser.'

support.prompt: Football tickets cost $45 each. What is the total cost of 3 tickets?
support.explanation: The total cost is 45 times the number of tickets, and 3 × 45 = 135.
feedback: $45 is the cost of just 1 ticket.
That adds 45 + 3 instead of multiplying 45 × 3.
$90 is the cost of 2 tickets, not 3.
hints: What is the cost of ONE ticket?
Each of the 3 tickets adds another $45.
Multiply the price of one ticket by the number of tickets.

support.prompt: Which ordered pair belongs on the ticket graph for 2 tickets?
support.explanation: The number of tickets goes first, and 2 tickets cost 2 × 45 = 90 dollars, so the point is (2, 90).
feedback: $45 is the cost of 1 ticket, not 2.
That adds 45 + 2 instead of multiplying 45 × 2.
You reversed the coordinates — the independent variable (tickets) goes first.
hints: Which quantity goes first in the ordered pair?
Tickets is the independent variable, so it comes first.
The second number is 2 × 45.

support.prompt: On the ticket graph, what should the two axes be labeled?
choices: Number of tickets and price of one ticket
Number of tickets and total cost
Number of games and number of tickets
support.explanation: Each axis is labeled with one quantity from the problem — one axis shows the number of tickets and the other shows the total cost.
feedback: The price of one ticket is fixed at $45 — it is not a changing quantity, so it does not get an axis.
$45 is a fixed rate, not a variable quantity that gets its own axis.
The number of games is not one of the two quantities in this problem.
hints: Which TWO quantities change in this situation?
One is the choice; the other responds to it.
You choose the tickets, and the total cost responds.

support.prompt: The Sandia Peak tram travels 1,200 feet each minute. How far has it traveled after 3 minutes?
support.explanation: The tram covers 1,200 feet every minute, so after 3 minutes it has gone 3 × 1,200 = 3,600 feet.
feedback: 1,200 feet is the distance after only 1 minute.
That adds 1,200 + 3 instead of multiplying 1,200 × 3.
2,400 feet is the distance after 2 minutes, not 3.
hints: How far does the tram go in ONE minute?
Each minute adds another 1,200 feet.
Multiply 1,200 by the number of minutes.

support.prompt: Predict the output for these settings.  Round to four decimal places if needed.
support.explanation: y = 2x + 4; when x = 3, y = 10. At x = 0, y = 4. Every increase of 1 in x adds 2 to y.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

support.prompt: A pattern starts with 4 fixed units and adds 2 units for every step. How many units are at step 6?
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

support.prompt: The same pattern follows y = 2x + 4. At what input x is y = 22?
support.explanation: Subtract the fixed 4, then divide by 2: (22 − 4) ÷ 2 = 9.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.prompt: A gym charges $24.95 per month. Which pair correctly names the variables?
core.explanation: You choose how many months to stay a member. The total cost responds to that.
feedback: You have the two variables backward. Ask which one someone gets to CHOOSE — that one is independent.
$24.95 is a fixed rate, not a variable that changes.
$24.95 is a fixed rate, not the responding quantity.
hints: Which number can the member change?
Months is the choice.
Cost responds to months.

core.prompt: Claire jogs 30 minutes and burns 123 Calories. At the same rate, how many Calories would a 90-minute jog burn?
core.explanation: 30 minutes burned 123 Calories, and 90 is 3 times 30, so the Calories are 3 times 123, which is 369.
feedback: 246 Calories is the 60-minute jog, not the 90-minute jog.
That is a rounded guess — scale 123 by the same factor as the time.
That is not the result of tripling 123.
hints: How many times longer is 90 minutes than 30 minutes?
90 divided by 30 is 3.
Multiply 123 by 3.

core.prompt: Which of these pairs is NOT a dependent relationship?
choices: Number of pizzas sold and weekly cost of cheese
Number of pizzas sold and number of employees the shop has
core.explanation: The shop has 6 employees whether it sells 5 pizzas or 500. That count does not respond to pizza sales.
feedback: Cheese cost DOES rise with more pizzas, so this pair is related.
Calories DO rise with more jogging, so this pair is related.
Cost DOES rise with more tickets, so this pair is related.
hints: Which one stays the same no matter what?
The staff list does not change when a pizza is sold.
Look for the pair that does not move together.

core.prompt: A plant grows 2 cm for every hour of daily sunlight. Which table row is correct?
core.explanation: At 2 cm per hour, 4 hours of sunlight gives 4 times 2, which is 8 cm.
feedback: That adds 2 instead of multiplying by 2.
That is the growth for a single hour, not for 4 hours.
That copies the number of hours instead of multiplying by the 2 cm rate.
hints: What does each hour add?
Each hour adds 2 cm.
4 hours means 4 groups of 2 cm.

core.prompt: The Sandia Peak tram travels 1,200 feet each minute and the ascent takes 15 minutes. How long is the whole ascent in feet?
feedback: That adds 1,200 + 15 instead of multiplying 1,200 × 15.
12,000 feet is the distance after 10 minutes, not the full 15.
16,800 feet is the distance after 14 minutes — one minute short of the top.
hints: How many minutes does the full ascent take?
Each of those 15 minutes covers 1,200 feet.
Multiply 1,200 by 15.

core.prompt: A table pairs hours with kilometers: (1, 48), (2, 96), (5, 240). How many kilometers are traveled each hour?
core.explanation: Each row is 48 times the number of hours: 2 × 48 = 96 and 5 × 48 = 240, so the rate is 48 kilometers per hour.
feedback: 24 splits the first rate in half, but the table shows a different distance in that very first hour.
96 km is the distance for 2 hours — divide it by 2 to get the rate for 1 hour.
240 km is the distance for 5 hours, not the per-hour rate.
hints: Look at the row for 1 hour.
Check it with another row: does 2 hours give twice as much?
The rate is the distance for exactly one hour.

core.prompt: Why is the line on the football ticket graph dashed instead of solid?
choices: Dashed lines always mean the cost is decreasing
The ticket price changes between points
You can only buy whole numbers of tickets, so the points between whole numbers do not make sense
core.explanation: You cannot buy 2.5 tickets, so only the whole-number points represent real purchases — the dashes show the trend without claiming the in-between points are possible.
feedback: The graph is complete — the dashes are a deliberate choice about what the in-between values mean.
Dashes say nothing about direction; this cost is increasing.
The price stays $45 per ticket everywhere on the graph.
hints: Could you buy half a ticket?
Which points on the line represent real purchases?
Only whole numbers of tickets make sense here.

core.prompt: The ticket table and ticket graph are two representations. Which statement about them is true?
choices: The graph shows a different relationship than the table
Only the table can show that cost increases with tickets
Only the graph is a real mathematical representation
Both show the same relationship — the table with numerical values, the graph in a more visual way
core.explanation: Every row of the table is plotted as a point, so both show cost = 45 × tickets — the table numerically, the graph visually.
feedback: Each point on the graph comes straight from a row of the table — they show the SAME relationship.
The graph also shows the increase: the points rise to the right.
Tables are just as mathematical as graphs — they show the same pairs of values.
hints: Where do the graph's points come from?
Each table row becomes one point.
Same pairs, two different pictures.

core.prompt: Predict the output for these settings.  Round to four decimal places if needed.
core.explanation: y = 3x + 4; when x = 3, y = 13. At x = 0, y = 4. Every increase of 1 in x adds 3 to y.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

core.prompt: A pattern starts with 4 fixed units and adds 2 units for every step. How many units are at step 6?
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.prompt: The same pattern follows y = 2x + 4. At what input x is y = 22?
core.explanation: Subtract the fixed 4, then divide by 2: (22 − 4) ÷ 2 = 9.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

stretch.prompt: Two quantities are related. Which statement is ALWAYS true?
choices: The independent variable is always the larger number
The independent variable is the input used to describe the relationship
The dependent variable is always measured in dollars
The independent variable is always listed first in a table
stretch.explanation: The independent variable is the input in the model. It may be chosen or observed; the dependent variable is described in relation to it. Size, units, and table position do not define its role.
feedback: A choice can be a small number — 1 hour is independent just as much as 100 hours.
Dependent variables can be centimeters, Calories, miles — anything that responds.
Table layout is a convention, not a definition.
hints: Which option restates the definition?
Definitions do not depend on size or units.
Look for the input used to describe how the other quantity changes.

stretch.prompt: Give an example where the SAME quantity can be independent in one problem and dependent in another.
choices: Time: chosen when you pick how long to jog, but measured as a result when you run a set distance
A quantity can never switch roles
stretch.explanation: Claire's two problems show exactly this: minutes is a choice in one and a result in the other.
feedback: Compare Claire's two jogs — in the 3-mile version time is the result.
In the 30-minute jog Claire chose the time, so it was independent there.
The role depends on the problem, not on the quantity itself.
hints: Look back at Claire's two problems.
In one she set minutes; in the other she set miles.
The role depends on what was chosen.

stretch.prompt: The pizza shop spends $1.15 on cheese per pizza. Which weekly total is correct if it makes 200 pizzas?
stretch.explanation: 200 pizzas at $1.15 each is 200 times 1.15, which is $230.
feedback: That is the cost for 100 pizzas, not 200.
That adds the numbers instead of multiplying them.
That multiplies as if each pizza cost $5.75.
hints: What operation joins a per-pizza cost and a count?
Multiply the rate by the number of pizzas.

stretch.prompt: Which relationship is NOT a case of one quantity depending on the other?
choices: A student's height and their house number
stretch.explanation: A house number is assigned by an address, not by how tall someone is — the two are unrelated.
feedback: More study time generally moves the score, so these are related.
These are related — the deck's own example.
These are related — more pizzas use more cheese.
hints: Which pair has no cause between them?
Would growing taller change your address?
Unrelated quantities have no dependence.

stretch.prompt: Nakai's savings account has a principal of $750 and earns 3.5% simple interest each year. How much interest does Nakai earn in one year?
stretch.explanation: One year of interest is 3.5% of $750: 0.035 × 750 = 26.25.
feedback: That treats 3.5% as $3.50 flat instead of taking 3.5% OF the $750 principal.
That is 10% of $750, not 3.5%.
That is 35% of $750 — the decimal point for 3.5% is one place further left.
hints: Write 3.5% as a decimal.
Multiply 0.035 by 750.

stretch.prompt: Nakai earns $26.25 in simple interest every year. On the graph of years vs. interest earned, which point represents 4 years?
stretch.explanation: After 4 years the interest earned is 4 × 26.25 = 105 dollars, so the point is (4, 105).
feedback: $26.25 is the interest for 1 year, not 4.
$78.75 is the interest after 3 years — one year short.
$750 is the principal Nakai deposited, not interest earned.
hints: How much interest arrives EACH year?
Four years means four equal payments of $26.25.
Multiply 26.25 by 4.

stretch.prompt: After 10 minutes, the Sandia Peak tram has traveled 12,000 feet. The whole ascent is 18,000 feet. How much farther must it travel to reach the top?
stretch.explanation: The remaining distance is 18,000 − 12,000 = 6,000 feet — which matches the last 5 minutes at 1,200 feet per minute.
feedback: 1,200 feet is only one more minute of travel — 5 minutes remain.
Check with the rate: 5 remaining minutes × 1,200 feet is 6,000, not 5,000.
12,000 feet is the distance already traveled, not what remains.
hints: How is 'distance remaining' related to the total?
Subtract the distance traveled from 18,000.
Check your answer: 5 minutes remain at 1,200 feet per minute.

stretch.prompt: A second tram travels 900 feet per minute. If both trams are graphed on the same axes (minutes vs. feet), how do the graphs compare?
choices: The 900 ft/min line rises more steeply
The Sandia Peak line (1,200 ft/min) rises more steeply than the 900 ft/min line
stretch.explanation: In one minute, the Sandia tram climbs 1,200 feet on the graph while the other climbs only 900 — a faster rate makes a steeper line.
feedback: Steepness follows the rate: 900 feet per minute rises LESS each minute than 1,200.
Different rates give different points — at 1 minute one graph is at 900 and the other at 1,200.
Both trams gain distance over time, so both lines rise.
hints: Compare where each graph is after 1 minute.
One is at 900 feet, the other at 1,200 feet.
The faster rate climbs more per minute — steeper.
